LANDLORD'S DUTY TO MITIGATE DAMAGES ON TENANT ABANDONMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet addresses what happens to a landlord's claim for unpaid rent and other damages under California Civil Code § 1951.2 if Jordan Lee breaches the lease and abandons the property at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield before August 31, 2027 — the end of the lease term that began September 1, 2026 — or if Acme Properties, LLC instead terminates Jordan Lee's right to possession because of a breach of the lease. It is a companion to the underlying lease between Acme Properties, LLC and Jordan Lee for that property, at a monthly rent of $2,200, and addresses only what happens to a landlord's damages claim after an abandonment or breach-based termination — not the lease terms themselves. This document states California statutory law and reported case law as of the date signed below. It does not determine that any breach, abandonment, or termination has occurred in this or any specific case, does not determine that any particular reletting effort was or was not reasonable, and does not calculate any landlord's actual recoverable damages.

WHEN A LANDLORD'S § 1951.2 DAMAGES CLAIM ARISES
Under California Civil Code § 1951.2, if a tenant breaches the lease and abandons the property before the end of the lease term — or if the tenant's right to possession is instead terminated by the landlord because of a breach of the lease — the lease terminates by operation of this statute. Upon that termination, the statute lets the landlord recover from the tenant the categories of damages the statute itself defines, described in the next clause of this document. This rule is stated as the general rule; a separate statute, Civil Code § 1951.4, provides an alternative remedy that a landlord may use instead in some circumstances, addressed later in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "if a lessee of real property breaches the lease and abandons the property before the end of the term or if his right to possession is terminated by the lessor because of a breach of the lease, the lease terminates."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the triggering events and general termination rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "Except as otherwise provided in Section 1951.4"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the section's own cross-reference to the alternative remedy in § 1951.4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  Known gap: This clause and the next several clauses in this document all draw on subdivisions of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1951.2 — they are not independent of one another. Section 1951.2 does not itself define "abandons" or "abandonment," and this document does not supply a definition beyond the statute's own text; whether a tenant has abandoned a specific property in a specific case is a factual question this document does not resolve. This is one state's statute; the remedies and mitigation rules that apply when a tenant abandons leased property vary by state, and this document addresses only California law.

THE FOUR CATEGORIES OF RECOVERABLE DAMAGES
Once a tenancy terminates under Civil Code § 1951.2, the statute lets the landlord recover, from the tenant, up to four categories of amounts: (1) the worth at the time of award of unpaid rent already earned before termination; (2) the worth at the time of award of unpaid rent that would have been earned between termination and the time of award, minus the amount of that rental loss the tenant proves could have been reasonably avoided; (3) — subject to a further condition addressed in a separate clause of this document — the worth at the time of award of unpaid rent for the remainder of the lease term after the time of award, minus the amount of that rental loss the tenant proves could be reasonably avoided; and (4) any other amount necessary to compensate the landlord for detriment proximately caused by the tenant's failure to perform the tenant's obligations under the lease, or that would likely result from that failure in the ordinary course of things. The statute also defines how "worth at the time of award" is computed: for categories (1) and (2), by allowing interest at the rate stated in the lease, or the legal rate if the lease states none; for category (3), by discounting the amount at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco's discount rate at the time of award, plus one percent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The worth at the time of award of the unpaid rent which had been earned at the time of termination"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, damages category 1 — rent already earned (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "The worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent which would have been earned after termination until the time of award exceeds the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could have been reasonably avoided"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, damages category 2 — rent between termination and award, minus avoidable loss (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "Subject to subdivision (c), the worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent for the balance of the term after the time of award exceeds the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could be reasonably avoided"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, damages category 3 — rent for the balance of the term, minus avoidable loss (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "Any other amount necessary to compensate the lessor for all the detriment proximately caused by the lessee’s failure to perform his obligations under the lease or which in the ordinary course of things would be likely to result therefrom."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, damages category 4 — other proximately caused detriment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "The “worth at the time of award” of the amounts referred to in paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (a) is computed by allowing interest at such lawful rate as may be specified in the lease or, if no such rate is specified in the lease, at the legal rate. The worth at the time of award of the amount referred to in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) is computed by discounting such amount at the discount rate of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco at the time of award plus 1 percent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, how "worth at the time of award" is computed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  Known gap: All five citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1951.2 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — not independent sources of one another. "Worth at the time of award" is a defined term of art under this statute, not an everyday-language damages figure; a specific landlord's actual recoverable amount in a specific case depends on proof (of unpaid rent, of the discount or interest rate that applies, and of any offset described in the following clauses) that this document does not supply or calculate.

THE MITIGATION OFFSET WITHIN THE RENT-DAMAGES CALCULATION
California's statute frames the landlord's duty to mitigate as a subtraction built into the rent-damages calculation itself, rather than as a separate, all-or-nothing bar on recovery. For damages categories (2) and (3) described in the preceding clause — unpaid rent between termination and the time of award, and unpaid rent for the remainder of the lease term — the statute allows the landlord to recover only the unpaid rent for the relevant period minus whatever amount of that rental loss could reasonably have been avoided. The statute places the burden of proving that a loss could have been reasonably avoided on the tenant, not the landlord, for both of those categories. Separately, the statute states that a landlord's own efforts to mitigate damages by attempting to relet the property do not waive the landlord's right to recover damages under this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could have been reasonably avoided"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, tenant's burden on the interim-period offset (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could be reasonably avoided"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, tenant's burden on the remaining-term offset (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "Efforts by the lessor to mitigate the damages caused by the lessee’s breach of the lease do not waive the lessor’s right to recover damages under this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, mitigation efforts do not waive the landlord's recovery (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on the same statutory section as the two clauses before it, Civil Code § 1951.2 (subdivisions (a) and (d)) — not independent of them. The mitigation offset described here applies only to damages categories (2) and (3); the statute's text states no equivalent offset for category (1), the rent already earned before termination. The statute's own text does not define what makes a rental loss one that "could have been reasonably avoided," and no such definition was found in § 1951.2 itself; a further condition on recovering category (3) damages specifically, and a court's discussion of the practical difficulty this burden allocation creates for tenants, are addressed in the next clause.

RECOVERING FUTURE-TERM RENT: THE RELETTING PRECONDITION AND BURDEN OF PROOF
The statute puts an additional condition on damages category (3) — unpaid rent for the balance of the lease term after the time of award. The landlord may recover that category of damages only if either: the lease itself provides for recovering it, using language about the amount by which unpaid rent for the balance of the term exceeds rental loss the tenant proves could be reasonably avoided; or the landlord relet the property before the time of award and proves that, in reletting it, the landlord acted reasonably and in a good-faith effort to mitigate the damages — in which case recovery under this category remains subject to any limitations stated in the lease. A California Court of Appeal, interpreting this statute, has observed that it places the tenant at a considerable procedural disadvantage on the mitigation issue: the burden is on the tenant to prove the landlord's reletting conduct was less than reasonable, even though exclusive possession and control of the property, and exclusive knowledge of what reletting efforts were or were not made, belong to the landlord.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The lease provides that the damages he may recover include the worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent for the balance of the term after the time of award, or for any shorter period of time specified in the lease, exceeds the amount of such rental loss for the same period that the lessee proves could be reasonably avoided"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, recovering category-3 damages by the lease's own terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "The lessor relet the property prior to the time of award and proves that in reletting the property he acted reasonably and in a good-faith effort to mitigate the damages, but the recovery of damages under this paragraph is subject to any limitations specified in the lease."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, recovering category-3 damages by actually reletting and proving reasonable, good-faith efforts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.2.)
  "section 1951.2 puts the lessee at a considerable procedural disadvantage in respect to the issue of mitigation of damages. The burden is placed on the lessee to prove the lessor’s conduct in attempting to relet was less than reasonable. However, exclusive possession and control of the premises and exclusive control over reletting efforts, including the knowledge of what efforts have or have not been made, are given exclusively to the lessor."
  — Desert Plaza Partnership v. Waddell, 180 Cal. App. 3d 805, 813–814 (1986), California Court of Appeal, Fourth District, on the tenant's procedural disadvantage under § 1951.2's mitigation burden (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2123426/desert-plaza-partnership-v-waddell/)
  Known gap: The two Civil Code citations below are both subdivision (c) of the same section, § 1951.2, quoted at length elsewhere in this document — not independent of those other citations. The Desert Plaza Partnership v. Waddell citation is an independently authored source, a published California Court of Appeal opinion rather than another subsection of the statute, but the quoted passage was offered by the court, in its own words, "although not at issue in this case" — it is the court's discussion of how the statute's burden allocation operates in practice, not the holding the court actually decided (the case turned on whether the parties had agreed to cancel the lease, a different question). Neither § 1951.2's text nor this case defines, with any checklist or numeric standard, what reletting efforts are "reasonable" or made in "good faith" — for example, neither source states that a landlord must use the same leasing efforts used for other units, advertise at a specific rent, or act within a specific number of days; no such statutory or judicial standard was found, and this document does not supply one.

THE ALTERNATIVE REMEDY: CONTINUING THE LEASE INSTEAD OF TERMINATING IT
Civil Code § 1951.2 states it applies "except as otherwise provided in Section 1951.4" — a separate statute giving landlords an alternative remedy. Under § 1951.4, even after a tenant has breached the lease and abandoned the property, the lease continues in effect for as long as the landlord does not terminate the tenant's right to possession, and the landlord may enforce the landlord's rights and remedies under the lease — including recovering rent as it becomes due — rather than pursuing the accelerated damages calculation under § 1951.2. This alternative remedy is available only if the lease itself provides for it, and, under the statute, only if the lease also permits the tenant to sublet the property or assign the tenant's interest in it. The statute further identifies specific landlord conduct that does not, by itself, count as terminating the tenant's right to possession for these purposes: maintaining or preserving the property, efforts to relet it, having a receiver appointed to protect the landlord's interest, and withholding or terminating consent to a subletting or assignment consistent with the tenant's rights under the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The remedy described in this section is available only if the lease provides for this remedy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, this remedy requires the lease to provide for it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.4.)
  "Even though a lessee of real property has breached the lease and abandoned the property, the lease continues in effect for so long as the lessor does not terminate the lessee’s right to possession, and the lessor may enforce all the lessor’s rights and remedies under the lease, including the right to recover the rent as it becomes due under the lease, if any of the following conditions is satisfied"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the lease continues in effect and rent may be recovered as it becomes due (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.4.)
  "For the purposes of subdivision (b), the following do not constitute a termination of the lessee’s right to possession: (1) Acts of maintenance or preservation or efforts to relet the property. (2) The appointment of a receiver upon initiative of the lessor to protect the lessor’s interest under the lease. (3) Withholding consent to a subletting or assignment, or terminating a subletting or assignment, if the withholding or termination does not violate the rights of the lessee specified in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, conduct that does not itself terminate the tenant's right to possession (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.4.)
  Known gap: Civil Code §§ 1951.4(a), (b), and (c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section — not independent of one another, and the § 1951.2 cross-reference quoted here, while textually located in a different Civil Code section, is the same section 1951.2 quoted at length elsewhere in this document. Section 1951.4(b) sets out three distinct ways a lease's sublet/assignment terms can qualify a landlord for this remedy, including a presumption (which the statute itself calls one "affecting the burden of proof") that a lease's own standards for consent to subletting are reasonable; this document states only the general condition — that the lease must permit subletting or assignment in some qualifying way — and omits that more granular sub-rule rather than state it imprecisely. This document does not determine whether any specific lease qualifies for this alternative remedy, and does not address which remedy — this one or the § 1951.2 damages remedy described elsewhere in this document — a landlord has elected in a specific case.

DAMAGES DOCUMENTATION WORKSHEET AND SIGNATURE
DAMAGES RECORD — 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield. Landlord: Acme Properties, LLC. Tenant: Jordan Lee. Lease term: September 1, 2026 to August 31, 2027. Monthly rent under the lease: $2,200. Date premises were abandoned or possession otherwise terminated: March 15, 2027.

For Landlord's own recordkeeping in connection with any claim under Civil Code § 1951.2: Unpaid rent earned before termination: $_______. Reletting efforts made (dates, methods, and asking rent): _______________________________________________. Date property was relet, if any: _______. Rent obtained upon reletting, if any: $_______.

This worksheet is a recordkeeping aid only. It does not calculate any amount owed, does not determine that any reletting efforts were reasonable, and does not constitute legal advice.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Acme Properties, LLC: _______________________ Date: _______________

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, conduct that does not itself terminate the tenant's right to possession
citations.quote: For the purposes of subdivision (b), the following do not constitute a termination of the lessee’s right to possession: (1) Acts of maintenance or preservation or efforts to relet the property. (2) The appointment of a receiver upon initiative of the lessor to protect the lessor’s interest under the lease. (3) Withholding consent to a subletting or assignment, or terminating a subletting or assignment, if the withholding or termination does not violate the rights of the lessee specified in subdivision (b).

expectedJSON.gap: Civil Code §§ 1951.4(a), (b), and (c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section — not independent of one another, and the § 1951.2 cross-reference quoted here, while textually located in a different Civil Code section, is the same section 1951.2 quoted at length elsewhere in this document. Section 1951.4(b) sets out three distinct ways a lease's sublet/assignment terms can qualify a landlord for this remedy, including a presumption (which the statute itself calls one "affecting the burden of proof") that a lease's own standards for consent to subletting are reasonable; this document states only the general condition — that the lease must permit subletting or assignment in some qualifying way — and omits that more granular sub-rule rather than state it imprecisely. This document does not determine whether any specific lease qualifies for this alternative remedy, and does not address which remedy — this one or the § 1951.2 damages remedy described elsewhere in this document — a landlord has elected in a specific case.
